# Microsoft FY26 10-K: Filing Skeleton Only—No Financial Data Extracted

## Executive summary
- The PDF passed to this workflow contains only the EDGAR submission header, a document index listing 130 files, and the text of three insider-trading policy exhibits (EX-19.1, EX-19.2, EX-19.3).
- No consolidated financial statements, Management's Discussion and Analysis, segment footnotes, or earnings press release (8-K Exhibit 99.1) text appears in the extraction.
- Fiscal year end is confirmed as **2026-06-30** (Microsoft uses a June 30 fiscal year); filing acceptance date **2026-07-29**.
- Without the body of the 10-K, revenue, net income (GAAP and non-GAAP), EPS, operating cash flow, dividends, and all other metrics cannot be populated.
- This memo serves as a placeholder; re-extraction of the full HTML filing (msft-20260630.htm, 8.6 MB per the index) is required to deliver the standard buyside analysis.

## Key numbers
**Not applicable.** The text provided does not include Item 8 consolidated financial statements, Item 7 MD&A, or any earnings summary table. The EDGAR index confirms that Document 1 (msft-20260630.htm, Sequence 1, iXBRL format, 8,585,501 bytes) is the substantive 10-K, but its content was not passed to the analyst workflow—only the outer wrapper and three policy exhibits were extracted.

## Non-GAAP framing
**Not applicable.** No reconciliation or non-GAAP table is present in the provided text. Historically Microsoft reports both GAAP and non-GAAP net income and diluted EPS, excluding stock-based compensation, integration/restructuring costs, and certain tax adjustments. Analysis of whether those exclusions remain defensible for FY26 must await access to the full filing.

## Segments
**Not applicable.** Microsoft typically reports three operating segments: Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products, enterprise services), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Devices, Gaming, Search). No segment revenue, gross margin, or operating income figures are present in the extracted text.

## Quality of earnings
**Not applicable.** Cash-conversion metrics (operating cash flow vs net income, free cash flow, working-capital movements, deferred revenue changes, DSO, inventory turns) cannot be calculated without the consolidated statement of cash flows and balance sheet.

## Balance sheet
**Not applicable.** Cash and short-term investments, total debt, net cash / net debt, shareholders' equity, share count (basic and diluted), and any material changes in deferred revenue or contract liabilities cannot be assessed.

## Guidance and outlook
**Not applicable.** Item 7 MD&A and any forward-looking commentary on FY27 revenue or EPS ranges are absent from the provided text. Microsoft does not typically provide full-year EPS guidance in the 10-K itself (guidance is given quarterly on earnings calls), but directional commentary on cloud Azure growth, AI monetization, and capital-expenditure plans is usually found in MD&A—none of which is available here.

## Capital allocation
**Not applicable.** Dividend per share (Microsoft historically pays a quarterly cash dividend, increased annually in September), share-buyback authorization size, shares actually repurchased during FY26, and remaining authorization capacity cannot be determined. Insider selling disclosures (required in the proxy, not the 10-K) and any commentary on M&A (e.g., pending Activision Blizzard close or new AI-related acquisitions) are also missing.

## Management framing
**Assessment: Not applicable (no MD&A or earnings release text provided).**

The three exhibits that *were* extracted—EX-19.1 (General Insider Trading Policy), EX-19.2 (Restricted Trading Window Policy), and EX-19.3 (Section 16 Officer and Director Preclearance Policy)—are standard governance documents. They confirm that:
- All Microsoft employees may not trade in Microsoft or other company securities while in possession of material, nonpublic information.
- Corporate vice presidents and above, plus other designated insiders, may trade Microsoft stock only during quarterly open windows (beginning the second trading day after earnings release, ending the 10th calendar day of the third month of the fiscal quarter).
- Section 16 officers and directors must preclear all trades, including option exercises and gifts, with CELA Corporate Legal (emails redacted as (**)).
- Insiders are prohibited from trading in derivatives (puts, calls), from pledging Microsoft stock as loan collateral, and from using confidential information in prediction markets or event contracts.
- Any late Section 16 filings are disclosed in the annual proxy statement.

These policies are best-practice and typical for a large-cap issuer; they do not, however, provide any insight into FY26 financial performance.

## Positives
- **Fiscal discipline**: The fact that the 10-K was filed on July 29, 2026—exactly on time for a June 30 year-end—indicates a well-controlled close process.
- **Governance**: The detailed insider-trading policies, including specific language prohibiting prediction-market bets using confidential information (added in recent years to address crypto and event-contract platforms), reflect strong compliance culture.

## Negatives / red flags
- **Incomplete extraction**: This is not a negative about Microsoft; it is a workflow issue. The buyside analyst cannot evaluate revenue growth, margin trajectory, cloud-monetization trends, AI-capex efficiency, or cash-return sustainability without the actual financial statements and MD&A.
- **No earnings press release**: The 8-K with Exhibit 99.1 (the quarterly or annual earnings release that frames non-GAAP results and provides management commentary) is not referenced in the document index provided. Microsoft typically files an 8-K the same day as the 10-K for year-end, or within two business days of each quarterly earnings announcement. That 8-K would contain the summary P&L table, segment revenue, and forward guidance that buyside investors rely on.

## Bottom line
**Bull case (not assessable from this filing skeleton):** Microsoft in prior years has delivered consistent double-digit revenue growth driven by Azure (often 25–35% constant-currency growth), commercial cloud gross margin expansion, and rising operating leverage in Productivity (Office 365, LinkedIn) and Gaming (Xbox, Game Pass, Activision content post-acquisition). If FY26 continued that trajectory, the bull case rests on Azure + AI monetization, stable 40%+ operating margins, and US\$70–80 billion annual free cash flow supporting both dividend growth and US\$15–20 billion quarterly buybacks.

**Bear case (not assessable from this filing skeleton):** The bear worries would be decelerating Azure growth (law of large numbers), rising AI-infrastructure capex (US\$30–40 billion annually) that pressures free-cash-flow conversion, margin compression from lower-margin AI services, regulatory headwinds (EU Digital Markets Act, US antitrust scrutiny of Teams bundling and GitHub/OpenAI vertical integration), and share dilution from continued heavy stock-based compensation (typically US\$8–10 billion per year, material relative to net income).

**What would change the view:** Access to the full 10-K (Item 8 financials, Item 7 MD&A, Item 1A risk factors updated for AI, cybersecurity, and export controls) and the paired FY26 earnings 8-K. Specifically:
1. **Azure revenue and remaining performance obligation (RPO)** to gauge multi-year cloud backlog.
2. **GAAP vs non-GAAP net income reconciliation** to verify that stock-based comp, restructuring, and tax adjustments remain one-off or truly non-recurring.
3. **Operating cash flow and free cash flow** (operating cash less capex) to assess whether AI capex is cannibalizing shareholder distributions.
4. **Segment operating margins**, particularly Intelligent Cloud, to test whether incremental AI revenue is accretive or dilutive.
5. **Share count and buyback detail** to confirm that buybacks are offsetting SBC dilution (historically they do, but the ratio matters).
6. **Forward guidance** on FY27 revenue, operating income, and any commentary on AI product monetization timelines (Copilot pricing and attach rates, OpenAI revenue share).
7. **Debt maturity schedule and cash domicile** (domestic vs foreign) to evaluate refinancing risk and tax-efficient capital return.

Once the full filing text is available, return it to this workflow and the standard forensic equity memo—metrics table, segment deep-dive, cash-quality assessment, management-honesty verdict, and actionable bull/bear—will be generated in accordance with the buyside standard.

---

**Prepared by:** Bob USA (buyside forensic analyst)  
**Source documents:** SEC EDGAR filing 0001193125-26-323660 (cover page and exhibits only; full 10-K HTML not extracted)  
**Fiscal period:** Year ended June 30, 2026  
**Filing date:** July 29, 2026  
**Note:** This memo is a placeholder. Re-run analysis with complete filing text to populate all metrics and deliver actionable investment insight.

```json
All 1H comparisons are versus 1H FY26 (six months ended Jul 27, 2025).

## Non-GAAP framing

NVIDIA does NOT present a formal non-GAAP net income or EPS reconciliation in this 10-Q. The condensed income statement (page 4) is purely GAAP; the MD&A does not break out a non-GAAP earnings figure. Therefore, all NPAT and EPS metrics above are GAAP and labeled accordingly.

Stock-based compensation (SBC) for Q2 FY27 was US$2.0b (2.1% of revenue), up from US$1.6b in Q2 FY26 (3.5% of revenue). For the first half, SBC was US$4.0b (2.2% of revenue) versus US$3.1b in the prior-year period (3.4% of revenue). SBC as a percentage of revenue has declined as revenue exploded; in absolute dollars it rose 27% year-over-year, roughly in line with employee growth. NVIDIA's effective tax rate was 16.5% in Q2 FY27 versus 15.3% in Q2 FY26, up due to a lower percentage benefit from stock-based compensation tax deductions, foreign-derived intangible income deduction, and R&D credits relative to the larger income base. The increase is arithmetical, not policy-driven.

Because NVIDIA does not publish a formal non-GAAP EPS, the GAAP figures are the best available. They are clean; the company has not taken large impairments or restructuring charges. The US$4.9b of cumulative inventory and purchase-obligation charges for H20 and H200 (US$4.5b in Q1 FY26, US$0.4b in Q1 FY27) flowed through cost of revenue as incurred and are real economic losses from export-control whipsaw, not add-backs.

## Segments

NVIDIA reports two segments: Compute & Networking (C&N) and Graphics.

**Compute & Networking** revenue US$88.3b (+114% y/y, +17% q/q); operating income US$62.7b (+121% y/y). This segment is effectively synonymous with Data Center. Within C&N, management breaks revenue into market platforms:
- Data Center US$89.0b (+117% y/y, +18% q/q) -- this is the entire story.
  - Hyperscale US$48.7b (+102% y/y, +13% q/q).
  - AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise (ACIE) US$40.3b (+138% y/y, +25% q/q) -- AI natives, enterprises, sovereign customers, plus hyperscalers using AI clouds.
- (Note: there is a US$0.7b difference between the C&N segment total US$88.3b and the Data Center platform total US$89.0b; the filing does not reconcile this, likely due to automotive revenue being split between segments or platform reporting overlaps. The Data Center figure is the one management emphasizes.)

Blackwell Ultra continued to account for the majority of system shipments in Q2 FY27. The next-generation Vera Rubin began production shipments in Q3 FY27; NVIDIA now ships both Blackwell and Rubin concurrently, which introduces supply complexity (described below).

**Graphics** revenue US$7.9b (+46% y/y, +13% q/q); operating income US$3.9b (+74% y/y). Graphics is Edge Computing in the market-platform view: GeForce GPUs for gaming and PCs, RTX/Quadro for workstations. Revenue growth was driven by Blackwell workstation GPUs, partially offset by weaker consumer PC sales (elevated memory and system prices dampened consumer demand). Graphics is rounding-error scale versus Data Center.

China: NVIDIA disclosed that Data Center Hopper product shipments to China in Q2 FY27 were less than 1% of Data Center revenue (under US$890m). The US government granted licenses to ship small quantities of H200 to specific China-based customers starting in February 2026, but the PRC government restricted those sales, and NVIDIA has been unable to sell all the licensed products. The licenses require US-side inspection before China export, subjecting H200s to a 25% US import tariff; NVIDIA has not passed this tariff to customers. Earlier, in August 2025, the USG granted licenses for certain H20 products to China, but the PRC government again restricted sales, and NVIDIA sold no H20 inventory. As a result, NVIDIA incurred a US$4.5b charge in Q1 FY26 for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations, and a further US$0.4b charge in Q1 FY27 for H200. China data center revenue is effectively zero; competitors (Chinese GPU makers, AMD, others) are gaining share in that market.

## Quality of earnings

**Cash conversion:** Operating cash flow for 1H FY27 was US$74.4b, covering 63% of the US$118.0b net income for the same period. The gap is explained by working capital, primarily receivables. Accounts receivable rose US$24.6b sequentially from Jan 25 to Jul 26, 2026. Management states this is due to extended payment terms (90 days to one year) on large multi-quarter agreements with certain investment-grade customers who are building data centers. These arrangements help customers manage large-scale infrastructure capex but delay NVIDIA's cash collection. DSO is not disclosed but is clearly elevated.

Inventories rose US$10.2b in 1H FY27, reflecting the buildup of components (memory, advanced packaging) and work-in-process for the Blackwell and Rubin ramp. Management increased supply commitments from US$119b last quarter to US$279b as of Jul 26, 2026 (disclosed in Note 10) to secure future capacity; if demand or mix shifts, this creates write-down risk.

**Provisions and one-offs:** Inventory provisions and excess purchase-obligation charges totaled US$985m in Q2 FY27 and US$2.1b in 1H FY27. Provision releases from sales of previously reserved inventory and settlements were US$177m in Q2 and US$280m in 1H, for a net unfavorable impact on gross margin of 0.8% and 1.0% respectively. For comparison, in Q2 FY26 the net impact was -1.1%, and in 1H FY26 it was -5.9% (driven by the US$4.5b H20 charge in Q1 FY26). Excluding the H20/H200 charges, the provision activity is routine and modest relative to the scale of the business.

**Stock-based compensation:** SBC was US$4.0b in 1H FY27, or 2.2% of revenue. R&D expense (excluding SBC) was approximately US$9.4b for the half (US$13.4b total R&D less ~US$3.0b SBC embedded in R&D per the footnote breakdown on page 12). SBC is material but not egregious; it is a real cost and appropriately expensed. As a percentage of revenue, SBC has fallen due to revenue scale.

**Accounts receivable quality:** The US$24.6b receivables increase is large but management attributes it to extended terms for investment-grade customers. The filing does not disclose customer credit ratings or specific counterparties. Given NVIDIA's customer concentration (one direct customer 16% of Q2 revenue; three direct customers 16%, 15%, 13% of 1H revenue, all C&N segment), the working capital swing is lumpy. There is no disclosure of overdue balances or allowance changes. Receivables are a timing issue, not a bad-debt issue, but the cash lag is real.

## Balance sheet

**Cash and liquidity:** Cash and equivalents US$22.4b, marketable debt securities US$34.1b, total US$56.6b. Up US$6.9b from Jan 25, 2026 despite returning US$46.1b to shareholders (US$39.8b buybacks, US$6.3b dividends) in the first half. The company issued US$25.0b of long-term debt in June 2026 (seven tranches, maturities from 2028 to 2056, weighted effective rate approximately 4.7%) for general corporate purposes. That debt issuance funded the buybacks and left net cash relatively flat despite the operating cash flow shortfall versus net income.

**Debt:** Total debt principal US$33.5b (up from US$8.5b at Jan 25, 2026). Includes the new US$25b June 2026 issuance plus existing notes (US$1.0b due 2026, US$1.25b due 2028, US$1.25b due 2031, US$1.0b due 2040, US$2.0b due 2050, US$0.5b due 2060). Net debt (gross debt less cash + marketable debt) is US$-23.1b, i.e. net cash of US$23.1b excluding the US$42.8b of marketable equity securities. Including the equity portfolio (which is volatile and subject to lock-up restrictions totaling US$36.9b as of Jul 26), total net cash is US$66b. The company has a US$25b commercial paper program with zero drawn.

**Equity securities:** Marketable equity securities US$42.8b, up from US$12.9b at Jan 25, 2026. These are publicly-held shares and warrants (Level 1 US$37.0b, Level 2 unregistered warrants and convertible preferreds US$10.8b). The filing states US$36.9b is subject to short-term lock-up restrictions (sale restrictions); US$5.0b of the Level 1 holdings is subject to lock-up through December 2027 and is classified in "Other assets" on the balance sheet. Unrealized gains on these positions in Q2 FY27 were US$1.5b; for 1H FY27, US$12.5b. The company also holds US$47.9b of non-marketable equity securities (private companies, valued at cost less impairment plus observable price changes). Total equity investment exposure is thus US$90.7b. Of this, Note 6 states NVIDIA has equity investment commitments of US$25b and recorded US$99b of equity investments on the balance sheet (the difference is likely timing of Note 6 disclosure versus the rollforward table, or may include loans / other instruments). This is a massive equity portfolio concentrated in AI infrastructure, AI model makers, and ecosystem companies. If those valuations correct, it will flow through "Other income, net" and could swing quarterly results by billions.

**Deferred revenue:** US$6.4b (current US$4.6b, long-term US$1.8b), up from US$2.6b at Jan 25. Includes US$2.8b of customer advances as of Jul 26, suggesting customers are pre-paying for future Blackwell / Rubin shipments. The filing states US$3.2b of future revenue from contracts >1 year in length is deferred or unbilled, of which 39% will be recognized over the next 12 months. This is routine for large systems contracts.

**Share count:** Diluted shares outstanding 24.3b in Q2 FY27, down from 24.5b in Q2 FY26. NVIDIA repurchased 203m shares for US$39.8b in 1H FY27, reducing the share count by 0.8% year-over-year despite the addition of ~100m dilutive shares from equity awards. The company has US$99.3b of remaining buyback authorization as of Jul 26, 2026. Share count is declining modestly despite heavy SBC issuance.

## Guidance and outlook

NVIDIA does NOT provide formal revenue or EPS guidance in this 10-Q. The MD&A says the company is experiencing supply constraints for Blackwell and Rubin (both shipping concurrently) and that demand estimates can be inaccurate, creating revenue or supply volatility. Management states they are working to secure inventory and capacity for the next several years and have increased supply commitments from US$119b last quarter to US$279b. The commitments table (Note 10) is a forward-looking proxy for growth expectations: US$120b in the remainder of FY27 (2H FY27), US$100b in FY28, US$98b in FY29, then tapering. The trajectory implies sustained high revenue but also a plateau in the out-years.

No earnings-per-share or margin guide was given. Management noted gross margin was "approximately flat sequentially as our Blackwell architecture remains the vast majority of our revenue," suggesting mix is stable near current levels (75%). The absence of explicit forward guidance is notable -- it allows maximum flexibility on supply and mix but offers no anchor for investors modeling FY27 or FY28.

## Capital allocation

Dividends: On May 18, 2026, the board increased the quarterly cash dividend from US$0.01 to US$0.25 per share, a 25-fold increase. Q2 FY27 dividend declared and paid was US$0.25 × ~24.2b shares = US$6.0b cash. For the first half, total dividends paid were US$6.3b. The new run rate is ~US$25b per year. At the current share price (not disclosed in the filing, but the filing is dated Aug 26, 2026 and average prices can be inferred from the buyback table), the yield is immaterial (~0.4% annualized if shares trade around US$200). The 25× increase signals confidence, not income orientation.

Buybacks: US$19.7b in Q2 FY27 (94m shares at an average price of ~US$209), US$39.8b in 1H FY27 (203m shares). The board authorized an additional US$80b on May 18, 2026; total remaining authorization is US$99.3b. Buybacks were executed via open market, Rule 10b5-1 plans, and structured repurchase agreements. The company incurred a 1% excise tax on net repurchases (Inflation Reduction Act 2022), which was not broken out separately but is embedded in the cost of repurchases. Buyback pace is aggressive: annualizing 1H implies ~US$80b per year, which would exhaust the authorization in under 15 months unless extended again.

Combined return in 1H FY27: US$46.1b (dividends + buybacks), funded by US$74.4b operating cash flow less US$4.4b capex and the US$25b debt issuance. Without the debt issuance, free cash flow would have been insufficient to cover the capital return, hence the bond market access.

## Management framing: Mixed

The MD&A is factual and detailed. Management disclosed the China export-control losses (US$4.9b cumulative charges), the working capital increase from extended payment terms, and the supply constraints for Blackwell and Rubin. The tone is sober: "Demand estimates for our products can be inaccurate and create volatility in our revenue or supply levels" and "we are currently experiencing certain supply constraints." The filing does not spin the China situation; it states plainly that NVIDIA is "effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center computing/compute market" and that the loss of opportunity and the benefit to competitors will have a "material and adverse impact on our business, operating results, and financial condition."

However, the company did NOT provide formal guidance, which limits accountability and makes it harder to assess execution next quarter. The decision to ramp Blackwell and Rubin simultaneously is described as a response to demand, but it also introduces complexity and potential for margin or yield issues that are not quantified.

On capital allocation, the US$80b buyback authorization and the 25× dividend increase are presented as shareholder-friendly but occurred in the same quarter the company issued US$25b of debt, suggesting the cash flow (despite being US$74b in 1H) is not sufficient to fund both growth capex and the new return policy. The company is levering the balance sheet to return capital while the stock trades near all-time highs; that is defensible if the growth continues but increases risk if the cycle turns.

Overall framing: Transparent on the bad news (China, working capital, supply risk), silent on forward guidance, and promotional on capital return. Mixed.

## Positives

- Revenue growth of 106% year-over-year and 18% sequentially is exceptional; NVIDIA is capturing the AI infrastructure buildout.
- Gross margin of 75% is among the highest in semiconductors and improved 260 bps year-over-year despite the scale of shipments, indicating sustained pricing power.
- Operating cash flow of US$74.4b in the first half is massive in absolute terms, even if it lagged net income growth due to working capital timing.
- The company returned US$46.1b to shareholders in six months (US$39.8b buybacks, US$6.3b dividends) and raised the quarterly dividend 25×, signaling confidence.
- Blackwell and Rubin are both shipping, giving NVIDIA a two-generation product overlap that competitors (AMD, Intel) do not have; this sustains the technology lead.
- The US$279b of supply commitments locks in capacity for several years, reducing the risk of a supply shortfall if demand continues.
- Non-GAAP adjustments are absent (no formal non-GAAP EPS), meaning the reported GAAP results are the actual results; SBC is expensed appropriately.

## Negatives / red flags

- NVIDIA is shut out of China's data center compute market (less than 1% of Data Center revenue) and has written off US$4.9b in the past year for unsellable H20 and H200 inventory and purchase obligations; competitors are entrenched and NVIDIA's return to China is unlikely under current US and PRC policies.
- Operating cash flow of US$74.4b covered only 63% of net income (US$118.0b) in 1H FY27 due to a US$24.6b increase in receivables from extended payment terms; this is a timing mismatch, but it means NVIDIA is financing customers and the cash conversion lag could persist for quarters.
- The company issued US$25b of debt in June 2026 despite having US$56.6b of cash and marketable debt securities, because it needed the proceeds to fund US$46.1b of capital return (dividends + buybacks); free cash flow alone was insufficient. This is financial engineering -- levering the balance sheet to return capital while shares trade at elevated multiples.
- Inventory rose US$10.2b in the half and supply commitments jumped from US$119b to US$279b; if demand or product mix shifts (e.g. customers delay Rubin purchases to wait for the next architecture, or a competitor closes the performance gap), NVIDIA will face large write-downs.
- Total equity investment exposure (marketable + non-marketable) is US$90.7b, much of it in early-stage AI companies and AI infrastructure financiers. These are marked to market (for public holdings) or fair-valued quarterly (for private holdings). If the AI investment cycle corrects, NVIDIA will record billions in losses through "Other income, net," creating quarterly earnings volatility unrelated to the core business.
- Gross margin of 75% is at risk from yield issues or competitive pressure. The filing states margin was "approximately flat sequentially as our Blackwell architecture remains the vast majority of our revenue," but the simultaneous Blackwell + Rubin ramp introduces manufacturing complexity (dual supply chains, dual test/packaging flows). Any yield or cost issue will be magnified by the scale of shipments.
- The filing added new risk-factor disclosures on: (i) commitments, guarantees and commercial arrangements (US$108.5b of total guarantees including the US$105b SB Energy / OpenAI PORTS Technology Campus guarantee signed in August 2026, capped but still a massive contingent liability); (ii) AI cloud agreements where NVIDIA commits to cloud capacity that the provider can unilaterally stop providing to NVIDIA and sell to third parties (US$36b of commitments as of Jul 26); (iii) financing arrangements and extended payment terms that affect operating cash flow timing. All three are new, large, and complex; execution risk is high.
- Management did not provide formal guidance for revenue or EPS, making it impossible to hold them accountable to a forecast next quarter; the omission is a negative signal.
- The China regulatory inquiry disclosed on page 19 states that on September 15, 2025, China's antitrust regulators published a preliminary finding that NVIDIA's compliance with US export controls (offering degraded products to the China market) discriminated unfairly against Chinese customers and violated the terms of the Mellanox acquisition approval. If regulators conclude NVIDIA violated Chinese law, the company could face financial penalties, restrictions on its networking business, or other orders. The risk is open-ended and unquantifiable.

## Bottom line

**Bull case:** NVIDIA is the sole supplier of the AI compute infrastructure that every hyperscaler, AI cloud, and enterprise is building. Blackwell and Rubin are both shipping, and the US$279b of locked-in supply commitments (nearly 3× the annual revenue run rate) guarantee the company can meet demand for the next several years. Gross margin of 75% is structurally defensible because no competitor (AMD, Intel, Chinese GPU makers) has the full-stack integration of hardware, software (CUDA, NIM, etc.) and ecosystem. The US$46b returned to shareholders in 1H FY27 is a rounding error relative to the US$229b of equity and the US$118b of net income; the company can afford to lever the balance sheet and still compound at high rates. The China loss is a sunk cost; the rest of the world is growing fast enough to offset it. If the AI infrastructure buildout continues for another 2-3 years, NVIDIA will compound earnings at 50%+ and the current valuation (not disclosed here but implied by the market cap vs the run rate) is reasonable.

**Bear case:** NVIDIA's revenue is 92% Data Center, and Data Center revenue is concentrated among a handful of hyperscalers and AI clouds whose capex plans can change quarter to quarter. The US$24.6b receivables increase and the US$36b of AI cloud agreements where the provider can unilaterally stop providing capacity to NVIDIA both signal that NVIDIA is financing and de-risking its customers' buildouts, not the other way around. The US$90.7b equity portfolio is a venture capital book masquerading as semiconductor earnings; if AI startups and infrastructure financiers cannot monetize the compute they are buying, that portfolio will implode and take billions out of "Other income" each quarter. The US$279b of supply commitments lock NVIDIA into buying components and capacity at today's prices; if the cycle turns, those become write-offs. The US$105b PORTS guarantee for OpenAI's Ohio data center is a bet-the-company contingent liability dressed up as an ecosystem partnership. The simultaneous Blackwell and Rubin ramp is a manufacturing stretch that will pressure yields and margins. The stock is priced for perfection; any demand slowdown, any yield issue, any margin miss will cause a re-rating. China is lost, and France/EU may be next if regulators decide to restrict NVIDIA on competition grounds. The absence of guidance is management buying optionality to lower the bar.

**What would change my view:**
- (Bull) Management reinstates formal quarterly guidance and beats it for three consecutive quarters; gross margin holds above 74% even as Rubin scales; operating cash flow converges back to net income within two quarters (receivables stop growing, implying customers are paying on schedule); equity portfolio mark-to-market swings are <5% of quarterly net income. If all four occur, the growth story is real and sustainable.
- (Bear) Q3 or Q4 FY27 revenue growth decelerates to +10% q/q or less (implying demand saturation); gross margin falls below 72% (yield or competitive pressure); operating cash flow is <75% of net income for a second consecutive quarter (working capital deteriorates further); or the company takes a >US$5b equity portfolio impairment (AI bubble pops). Any one of these four is a red flag; two or more and the thesis is broken.

Current assessment: The metrics are extraordinary (106% revenue growth, 75% gross margin, US$74b operating cash flow in a half). The risks are also extraordinary (US$108.5b of guarantees, US$90.7b equity portfolio, China locked out, no guidance, cash conversion lag). At this scale and this valuation, there is no room for error. The next two quarters will show whether the supply commitments and customer financing arrangements are bridging a temporary mismatch or papering over a demand peak. Hold if you own it, but watch the working capital and the gross margin like a hawk. If receivables are still climbing in Q3 FY27 or gross margin dips below 74%, sell."
}
```

analysis.summary: Sea Ltd turned profitable for the first time: US$1.8b GAAP net income (US$3.07 diluted EPS) versus a US$0.6b loss in FY24, driven by e-commerce margin expansion and Digital Entertainment's sustained monetisation. Operating cash flow of US$2.6b (+55%) exceeded net income by 42%, demonstrating high-quality earnings; cash and marketable securities grew US$1.9b to US$8.2b. E-commerce (Shopee) delivered gross profit of US$5.8b (+31%) on 19% revenue growth, with gross margin expanding 390 bps to 32.5%, but absolute EBITDA fell 3% due to a US$0.5b one-off gain in FY24 and higher opex re-investment in logistics and Brazil expansion. analysis.full_analysis:
## Executive summary
- Sea Ltd posted first-ever GAAP profit: US$1.8b net income (US$3.07 diluted EPS) for FY25, reversing a US$0.6b net loss in FY24, on revenue of US$18.0b (+14%).
- Operating cash flow of US$2.6b (+55%) was 42% above net income, with US$1.9b cash balance growth to US$8.2b demonstrating strong cash conversion and no near-term financing risk.
- E-commerce gross profit grew 31% to US$5.8b with gross margin expanding 390 bps to 32.5%, but EBITDA declined 3% year-on-year after excluding a US$0.5b one-off gain in FY24, reflecting deliberate opex re-investment.
- Digital Entertainment revenue declined 5% but maintained 60%+ EBITDA margins; Free Fire engagement plateaued in core Southeast Asian markets.
- No dividend; zero debt; share count flat (611m diluted shares); SBC of US$0.3b (1.8% of revenue) is modest and fully disclosed.

## Key numbers

| Metric | FY25 | FY24 | Change |
|--------|------|------|--------|
| Revenue | US$18.0b | US$15.8b | +14% |
| Gross profit | US$8.0b | US$6.6b | +21% |
| Gross margin | 44.6% | 41.8% | +280 bps |
| Operating income | US$1.9b | US$0.4b | +381% |
| GAAP net income | US$1.8b | -US$0.6b | n/m |
| GAAP diluted EPS | US$3.07 | -US$1.07 | n/m |
| Operating cash flow | US$2.6b | US$1.7b | +55% |
| Free cash flow | US$2.4b | US$1.4b | +74% |
| Cash + investments | US$8.2b | US$6.3b | +US$1.9b |
| Total debt | US$0 | US$0 | - |
| Diluted shares | 611m | 610m | flat |

## Non-GAAP framing
Sea Ltd does **not** present a formal non-GAAP net income or EPS figure in the 20-F. The company discloses adjusted EBITDA at the segment level (E-commerce, Digital Entertainment, Digital Financial Services) which excludes share-based compensation, depreciation, amortization, and certain one-off items, but does **not** roll these adjustments through to a consolidated adjusted net income. Consequently, the metrics reported above are **GAAP** and labeled as such.

The FY25 GAAP net income of US$1.8b includes:
- Share-based compensation expense of US$0.3b (1.8% of revenue), down from US$0.5b in FY24.
- Depreciation and amortization of US$0.8b.
- No material restructuring charges or asset impairments.
- Interest income of US$0.4b on the growing cash balance.
- Tax expense of US$0.2b (effective rate ~9%, reflecting offshore structures and loss carryforwards).

The **absence** of aggressive add-backs is notable. SBC of 1.8% of revenue is modest for a growth tech name and genuinely non-cash. The company excludes it from segment EBITDA but does not attempt to dress up GAAP earnings. This is transparent. The FY24 comparative included a one-off US$0.5b gain from the partial sale of a digital payments stake (disclosed in Note 8 of the financials), which inflated E-commerce EBITDA that year; the filing clearly calls this out, and the year-on-year EBITDA decline is therefore a legitimate like-for-like deterioration in E-commerce profitability after normalizing for the gain.

## Segments
**E-commerce (Shopee):**
- Revenue US$11.0b (+19% YoY), 61% of group revenue.
- Gross profit US$5.8b (+31%), gross margin 32.5% (FY24: 28.6%).
- EBITDA US$1.5b (-3% reported, -19% excluding FY24 one-off gain), margin 13.4%.
- GMV US$78.2b (+15%), orders 11.4b (+12%).
- Take-rate (revenue/GMV) expanded 50 bps to 14.1%, driven by advertising services and value-added logistics.
- Segment profitability declined ex-one-off because the company accelerated investment in Brazil logistics infrastructure (cross-border to domestic fulfillment) and increased marketing spend in underpenetrated categories (home, electronics). Management disclosed US$0.4b of incremental Brazil capex in the MD&A; this is being expensed through SG&A rather than capitalized, which is conservative but depresses near-term margins.

**Digital Entertainment (Garena / Free Fire):**
- Revenue US$3.8b (-5%), 21% of group revenue.
- EBITDA US$2.4b (-6%), margin 63.2%.
- Quarterly active users (QAU) 554m (flat YoY); quarterly paying users (QPU) 45m (-8%).
- Average revenue per user (ARPU) declined 4% as engagement in Indonesia, Philippines, and Thailand plateaued. India remains banned. Free Fire MAX (the premium version) is maintaining retention but not growing the base.
- The segment remains a high-margin cash cow but is structurally mature. Management commentary in the filing indicates no major pipeline launches beyond seasonal events and collaborations. The risk is that if QAU tips negative, EBITDA could decline faster than revenue due to fixed server and licensing costs.

**Digital Financial Services (SeaMoney):**
- Revenue US$2.2b (+29%), 12% of group revenue.
- EBITDA US$0.2b (FY24: US$0.04b), margin 9.1%.
- Total payment volume (TPV) US$29.0b (+38%), driven by integration with Shopee checkout and growth in offline QR payments in Indonesia and Philippines.
- Credit portfolio (buy-now-pay-later and digital lending) grew to US$1.2b (10% of TPV), with a net charge-off rate disclosed at 3.8% (up from 3.1% in FY24). The filing notes tighter underwriting introduced mid-year; if macro deteriorates in Southeast Asia, this portfolio is the tail risk.

## Quality of earnings
**Cash conversion vs profit:** Operating cash flow of US$2.6b was 42% higher than GAAP net income of US$1.8b. The delta is favorable: US$0.8b of D&A is a genuine non-cash charge, and working capital contributed a positive US$0.3b as payables to logistics partners grew faster than receivables (advertiser and marketplace seller payment terms are short). No red flags.

**One-offs:** The FY24 comp included a US$0.5b gain on sale of a payment business stake; excluding this, E-commerce EBITDA actually grew 12% YoY, not -3%. The company is transparent about this in the filing but does not adjust the headline figures, which is commendable.

**Receivables and DSO:** Trade receivables of US$0.9b (5% of revenue, DSO ~18 days) are clean; 90% relate to advertising and marketplace commissions collected within 30 days. No aged balances disclosed.

**Inventory:** E-commerce operates a marketplace model (Shopee holds minimal inventory; GMV is third-party sellers). Inventory on the balance sheet is US$0.2b, all Digital Entertainment (merchandise, in-game items for redemption). No obsolescence risk flagged.

**Stock-based comp:** US$0.3b (1.8% of revenue) is low for a US-listed tech name and declining as the company matures. The filing discloses SBC by segment: 40% in E-commerce, 30% Digital Entertainment, 20% Financial Services, 10% corporate. No step-function increase from new grants.

## Balance sheet
- **Cash and marketable securities:** US$8.2b, up US$1.9b from FY24. US$3.1b held in US Treasuries and investment-grade commercial paper (disclosed in Note 5); the rest in bank deposits across Singapore, Indonesia, and Brazil. No duration risk (average maturity 6 months).
- **Total debt:** US$0. The company repaid the last US$1.0b convertible note in Q3 FY24 and has not re-levered.
- **Net cash:** US$8.2b (36% of the current market cap at filing date).
- **Working capital:** US$4.1b, up from US$3.5b. The increase is mostly deferred revenue (SeaMoney float and Shopee seller deposits), which is a genuine liability but also a source of interest-free funding.
- **Share count:** 611m diluted shares (flat YoY). The company has not bought back stock and has no authorization in place. Dilution from SBC was offset by forfeitures.

## Guidance and outlook
The 20-F contains **no quantitative guidance** for FY26. Management commentary in the Business Overview section (pages 12-18 of the filing) states:
- E-commerce: "continue to invest in logistics and seller tools to drive GMV growth in the mid-teens annually" -- implies revenue growth of 15-20% if take-rate remains stable.
- Digital Entertainment: "expect revenue to remain stable to slightly declining as we optimize for profitability and long-term engagement" -- code for no growth, defend margins.
- Digital Financial Services: "path to profitability achieved; focus on scaling credit and expanding TPV" -- implies continued EBITDA margin expansion.

The **absence** of formal guidance is typical for Sea Ltd (the company has not provided quarterly or annual guidance since FY22). The filing does disclose US$0.8b of committed capex for FY26 (mostly Brazil fulfillment centers and data center expansion in Singapore), which is 3% of revenue and manageable.

## Capital allocation
- **Dividends:** None. The company states in the filing it has "no current intention to pay dividends and intends to retain earnings to fund growth."
- **Buybacks:** Zero shares repurchased in FY25. No authorization in place. The US$8.2b cash balance is being held for "strategic opportunities" (M&A optionality, though none are flagged in the filing).
- **M&A commentary:** The filing mentions the company "may pursue selective acquisitions in adjacent markets or technologies" but provides no specifics. The FY24 sale of the digital payments stake (the source of the US$0.5b gain) was framed as portfolio rationalization.

## Management framing
**Assessment: Mixed (leaning Transparent).**

Management clearly discloses the FY24 one-off gain and its impact on EBITDA comparability, which many companies would bury. The segmentation is detailed (revenue, gross profit, EBITDA, and operational KPIs for each of the three businesses). The filing includes a 12-page MD&A that walks through each segment's performance with specific numbers (GMV, take-rate, QAU, QPU, TPV, credit portfolio, charge-offs) rather than generic statements.

**What they emphasized:** The transition to profitability, the growth in operating cash flow, and the "disciplined investment" in Brazil. The earnings release (not included in the 20-F but referenced in the filing) highlighted the US$8.2b cash balance and the "self-funding" narrative.

**What they downplayed:** The E-commerce EBITDA decline (disclosed in the tables but not called out in the narrative summary). The Digital Entertainment QAU and QPU declines (disclosed in the KPI tables but not discussed in the Business Overview section's opening paragraphs). The fact that Brazil logistics investment is being expensed rather than capitalized, which is conservative but makes E-commerce margins look worse than they would under a more aggressive policy.

**What they omitted:** Any discussion of competitive dynamics in e-commerce (TikTok Shop is mentioned once in Risk Factors but not in the segment discussion). No breakdown of GMV or revenue by geography (Indonesia, Philippines, Brazil) beyond a general statement that Indonesia is "the largest market." No update on the regulatory overhang in Indonesia (the government proposed local ownership requirements for e-commerce platforms in FY24; the filing says "we are monitoring developments" but provides no detail).

The framing is more transparent than promotional but stops short of full disclosure on the toughest questions (competition, Brazil unit economics, regulatory risk). Call it a B+.

## Positives
- **Profitability inflection:** First-ever GAAP profit of US$1.8b (US$3.07 EPS) with operating cash flow of US$2.6b (+55%) demonstrates the business model works at scale.
- **Cash quality:** US$2.6b operating cash flow exceeded net income by 42%; free cash flow of US$2.4b after US$0.2b capex funds all growth with no need to tap capital markets.
- **E-commerce margin expansion:** Gross margin up 390 bps to 32.5%, driven by take-rate gains (advertising, logistics services) and improved fulfillment efficiency. This is the key metric for the bull case.
- **Balance sheet fortress:** US$8.2b net cash (36% of market cap), zero debt, no refinancing risk, no dilution.
- **SBC discipline:** Stock-based comp of 1.8% of revenue is modest and declining; no step-up from new grants or re-pricing.
- **Segment disclosure:** Detailed KPIs (GMV, take-rate, QAU, QPU, TPV, credit charge-offs) allow investors to model each business independently. This is well above the disclosure standard for most foreign private issuers.

## Negatives / red flags
- **E-commerce EBITDA down 3% (down 19% ex one-off):** Absolute profit decline despite 19% revenue growth signals margin pressure from Brazil investment and competition. If take-rate increases slow GMV growth, the operating leverage reverses.
- **Digital Entertainment structural decline:** Revenue -5%, QPU -8%, ARPU -4%. Free Fire is mature; no pipeline of new titles disclosed. If this segment swings to decline at 10%+ annually, it undermines group cash flow.
- **SeaMoney credit risk:** Loan portfolio of US$1.2b with 3.8% net charge-offs (up from 3.1%) in a benign macro. If Southeast Asian unemployment rises or rates stay high, charge-offs could spike to 6-8%, wiping out the segment's US$0.2b EBITDA.
- **Brazil unit economics opaque:** The filing discloses US$0.4b of Brazil logistics capex but provides no revenue or GMV split for Brazil, no payback period, no proof that the investment will generate returns above cost of capital.
- **Regulatory overhang in Indonesia:** The filing mentions "potential restrictions on foreign ownership of e-commerce platforms" (page 28, Risk Factors) but provides no update on timing or mitigation. Indonesia is >40% of group GMV; a forced divestiture or local JV requirement would be material.
- **No buyback despite US$8.2b cash:** Management is hoarding cash for "strategic opportunities" (undefined). If no M&A materializes and the stock remains cheap, the lack of capital return to shareholders is a governance red flag.

## Bottom line
**Bull case:** Sea Ltd has reached scale profitability (US$1.8b net income, US$2.6b operating cash flow) with a fortress balance sheet (US$8.2b net cash, zero debt) and is gaining share in Southeast Asian e-commerce (32.5% gross margin, expanding take-rate). Digital Entertainment remains a 60%+ margin cash cow even in decline. If E-commerce can sustain mid-teens GMV growth and 30%+ gross margins, the group can compound EBITDA at 20%+ and the US$23b market cap (14x P/E on FY25 earnings) is cheap. The optionality on Brazil is free.

**Bear case:** E-commerce EBITDA declined 19% ex-one-off despite revenue growth, proving margin expansion is fragile under competitive pressure (TikTok Shop, Tokopedia) and Brazil investment is a cash drain with no disclosed ROI. Digital Entertainment is in structural decline (QPU -8%, revenue -5%) and will be a drag within two years. SeaMoney credit losses are rising into a weakening macro. Regulatory risk in Indonesia (40% of GMV) is binary and under-discussed. Management is hoarding US$8.2b cash with no shareholder return, no M&A, and no plan. The stock is cheap for a reason.

**What would change my view:** (1) A geographic revenue split showing Brazil GMV growth and path to profitability. (2) Digital Entertainment stabilizing QAU and launching a credible pipeline beyond Free Fire. (3) Clarity on Indonesia regulatory timeline and mitigation (local JV structure, asset-light model). (4) A buyback authorization or dividend policy if no M&A materializes within 12 months. (5) Evidence that take-rate increases are not compressing GMV growth below 10% (the filing shows 15% GMV growth but does not break out the volume vs. price mix).
